items.q: The normal serum phosphorus range used in this chapter is ___ mg/dL.
items.exp: The page gives 2.5–4.5 mg/dL; values above 4.5 are classified as hyperphosphatemia. (Book p887)

items.q: A stable patient has phosphate 1.8 mg/dL without symptoms. How does the opening severity diagram classify this value?
items.exp: The 1–2.5 mg/dL branch is described as asymptomatic without routine treatment in this simplified diagram. Later pages discuss oral replacement; decisions depend on cause and clinical context. (Book p887)

items.q: Which phosphate level crosses the chapter's severe-depletion threshold rather than merely its low-reference threshold?
items.exp: The severe phosphorus-depletion branch is <1 mg/dL. (Book p887)

items.q: Assess: I Most body phosphorus is in the inorganic extracellular pool. II Routine serum phosphorus predominantly measures inorganic extracellular phosphate.
items.exp: The forms tree separates the larger organic intracellular pool from inorganic HPO4 in extracellular blood, the pool measured in serum assays. (Book p887)

items.q: Match the following phosphorus compartments — 1) Bone 2) Soft tissue 3) Extracellular fluid … A) 85% B) 14% C) 1%
items.exp: The phosphorus column allocates 85% to bone, 14% to soft tissue and 1% to ECF. (Book p887)

items.q: Total body stores in the comparison table are about ___ calcium versus ___ phosphorus.
items.exp: The table contrasts approximately 1200 g of calcium with 500–800 g of phosphorus. (Book p887)

items.q: Match the following calcium compartments — 1) Bone 2) Soft tissue 3) ECF … A) 99.3% B) 0.6% C) 0.1%
items.exp: The calcium distribution is 99.3% bone, 0.6% soft tissue and 0.1% extracellular, distinct from the phosphate distribution. (Book p887)

items.q: Albumin falls in a patient whose calcium and phosphate are both measured. Which correction approach follows the comparison table?
opts: Consider calcium correction; do not use a corrected-phosphate formula
Apply the same albumin correction to both minerals
Correct phosphate only because its binding is greater
Ignore albumin because both minerals are entirely free
items.exp: The table gives 40% albumin binding for calcium versus 10% for phosphorus and states there is no role for corrected phosphorus. (Book p887)

items.q: Albumin-bound fractions are approximately ___ for calcium and ___ for phosphorus.
items.exp: These fractions explain why albumin correction is discussed for calcium but not routinely for phosphate. (Book p887)

items.q: Match the following — 1) Main calcium/phosphate absorption site in the source 2) Magnesium absorption site 3) Calcium absorption protein … A) Jejunum B) Ileum C) Calbindin
items.exp: The page groups calcium and phosphate with jejunal absorption, names the ileum for magnesium and includes calbindin in calcium handling. (Book p887)

items.q: The net intestinal absorption fractions in the comparison are calcium ___ and phosphorus ___.
items.exp: The table shows 20% net calcium absorption and 60% net phosphorus absorption. (Book p887)

items.q: Evaluate: I The source splits phosphate absorption into 80% active and 20% passive. II It splits calcium absorption into 95% active and 5% passive.
items.exp: These are the chapter's contrasting active/passive fractions; the active phosphate arm is labeled vitamin-D dependent. (Book p887)

items.q: A student says the page's shared absorption sketch proves that calbindin transports phosphate directly. Which correction is most appropriate?
opts: Vitamin D promotes both; calbindin specifically supports calcium handling
Calbindin is the principal renal phosphate cotransporter
Phosphate is absorbed only by passive diffusion
Vitamin D has no intestinal phosphate effect
items.exp: The schematic groups vitamin D and the two minerals, but calbindin should not be misidentified as the sodium–phosphate transporter. It is a calcium-binding protein, not vitamin-D-binding protein despite the handwritten label. (Book p887)
